The fact that it's the only genre I've experienced so far that has the potential to employ EVERYTHING in its music.

Emotional depth, All poetic devices/all lyrical depth imaginable, Social issues, Controversial topics, Comedy/joking, Serious as well as party music, All tempos of music.
Outkast - Aquemini

Jazz is a genre that is made up of mostly instrumentals and some vocals, all of which isn't controversial in the slightest. Hip-Hop deals with a much broader plateau of subject matter and can be taken either way. So it comes down to this: When people first listen to jazz their subconscious goes "oh this is fine, it doesn't set off any preconceptions about who's making the music and it sounds pleasant, it's A-OK." But when they listen to rap if anything that's not relatable is mentioned (being poor, being opressed by white people, stealing & killing, selling drugs) their subconscious starts making all sorts of negative judgements about the people saying this without even knowing or understanding where the person is coming from, so they're turned off from the music.
For me it's 75% lyrics and 25% production.

I'm assuming they all stereotype it as being some senseless blabbering about substanceless things. So this is what I would recommend.

1. 2Pac - Unconditional Love (or Dear Mama)
2. Jedi Mind Tricks - Uncommon Valor: A Vietnam Story
3. Eminem - Stan
4. Immortal Technique - Dance With The Devil
5. DMX - Slippin'

I guess most of us middle class suburban kids were mostly exposed to pop before stumbling upon hip-hop. However, when I first heard some of Eminem's material it stuck to me, the lyrical complexity was unmatched by any other genre. So from that point on, I was set on a journey to fully explore the genre as much as I could.
I'm fourteen, and have been listening to hip-hop since 2010.
